papers.title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

papers.title: Approximate Computation via Le Cam Simulability
papers.abstract: We propose a decision-theoretic framework for computational complexity, complementary to classical theory: moving from syntactic exactness (Turing / Shannon) to semantic simulability (Le Cam). While classical theory classifies problems by the cost of exact solution, modern computation often seeks only decision-valid approximations. We introduce a framework where "computation" is viewed as the efficient simulation of a target statistical experiment within a bounded risk distortion (Le Cam deficiency). We formally define computational deficiency ($\delta_{\text{poly}}$) and use it to construct the complexity class LeCam-P (Decision-Robust Polynomial Time), characterizing problems that may be syntactically hard but semantically easy to approximate. We show that classical Karp reductions can be viewed as zero-deficiency simulations, and that approximate reductions correspond to bounded deficiency. Furthermore, we establish the No-Free-Transfer Inequality, showing that strictly invariant representations inevitably destroy decision-relevant information. This framework offers a statistical perspective on approximation theory, bridging the gap between algorithmic complexity and decision theory.

papers.title: Efficient Recursive Evaluation of Gaussian, Gamma, and Inverse Gaussian Tail Probabilities
papers.abstract: Accurate computation of tail probabilities motivates efficient high-order implementations of the $G_n^{(1)}$ extrapolation transformation. We derive finite recurrence relations in the transformation order for Gaussian, gamma, and inverse Gaussian tail approximations. The Gaussian and inverse Gaussian numerator and denominator sequences satisfy four-term recurrences, whereas the gamma sequences satisfy a three-term recurrence. The derivation exploits the structure of the underlying differential operator and shows that the reduced numerator and denominator obey recurrences with identical coefficients. This construction avoids the repeated evaluation of higher-order derivatives and nested sums required by the explicit formulations. As a result, generating the approximation sequence through order $n$ requires $O(n)$ arithmetic operations, compared with $O(n^3)$ for the Gaussian and gamma distributions and $O(n^4)$ for the inverse Gaussian distribution. The recurrence algorithms also require only a fixed number of previously computed quantities at each order. Numerical results for the three distributions are in excellent agreement with values reported in the literature

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Channel Coding
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for the study and evaluation of the fundamental limits of channel coding, emphasizing genuinely nonasymptotic results. The {\em channel coding sample complexity} $n^*({\cal W},\epsilon)$ of a channel ${\cal W}$ is defined as the smallest blocklength at which it is possible to transmit information through that channel with error probability below $\epsilon$ and at a rate at least as high as that given by an appropriate constraint also in terms of $\epsilon$. This formulation follows analogous developments in statistics, computer science and, more recently, in lossless source coding. For any discrete memoryless channel we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the sample complexity, with explicit constants. These bounds show that the sample complexity is characterized not by the usual channel capacity, but by the channel's Augustin--Csisz\'{a}r capacity of order $1/2$, which coincides with the cutoff rate as well as with the channel's Sibson capacity of order $1/2$. The proof is partly based on a new channel-coding one-shot converse in terms of hypothesis testing. We also examine extensions of the sample complexity framework to general target rates. Moreover, we derive corresponding results for the sample complexity of the additive white Gaussian noise channel with a quadratic power constraint. Their proof relies on new, explicit upper bounds on the best achievable error probability, which may be of independent interest.

papers.title: High-dimensional limit theorems for adaptive variants of SGD I: Ballistic limits
papers.abstract: We develop the high-dimensional effective dynamics for adaptive, momentum-based variants of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). These effective dynamics are given by a Markov process. They key observation is that the non-Markovianity in the algorithm due to the exponential moving average and preconditioning can be treated using the method of averaging. Our approach applies to a broad class of algorithms including to Adaptive momentum estimation (ADAM), Momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schultz (MUON), and its variants. It also applies to a broad class of learning tasks, such at tensor PCA, Gaussian projective models, teacher-student networks, and a multi-layer neural network trained on the XOR problem using a hybrid of MUON and ADAM as commonly done in practice. We demonstrate how to this technique can give precise, quantitative comparisons between algorithms. In particular, we find interesting phenomena, such as the cross-over phenomenon where online SGD has better generalization than ADAM early in training until the learning curves cross and ADAM dominates. Furthermore, we prove a version of the Edge of Stability phenomenon. In particular, we introduce an analogue of the infinity Laplacian that sharply characterizes the Edge of Stability.

papers.title: Log-optimal two-sample testing by betting
papers.abstract: For each standard Borel observation space, we construct a single anytime-valid two-sample procedure that is asymptotically log-optimal for every pair of unknown probability laws and every limiting ratio of diverging sample sizes, including zero and infinity. For independent balanced pairs, the optimal log-wealth rate is $2\JS(P,Q)$, where $\JS$ is the Jensen--Shannon divergence. Unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen--Shannon information and the one-sample limit $\log W(n_1,n_2)/n_2\to\KL(Q\|P)$ when $n_1/n_2\to\infty$. Refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels provide universal constructions. Our main contribution is the generality of our construction, and its connections to classical batch efficiency notions. Practical implementations allow continuous classifier fine-tuning, as demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.

papers.title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
papers.abstract: We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

papers.title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

papers.title: Phase Transitions in Heavy-Tailed Mean Estimation under $\ell_p$ Norms
papers.abstract: We study the problem of estimating the mean of a random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ under $\ell_p$ norms, assuming only the existence of a covariance matrix. In the Euclidean norm, the sample mean is already optimal in expectation, and robust estimators are usually needed only to obtain high-probability tails. Our results show that this picture changes for $\ell_p$ norms with $p>2$: robustification is already necessary even for the expected risk. We prove that the minimax risk exhibits a sharp phase transition, controlled by the interaction between the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, and the norm parameter $p$. In the large-sample regime, the classical Gaussian rate remains achievable. In the complementary regime, heavy-tailed distributions create a genuinely non-Gaussian obstruction. Furthermore we show that the simple estimator: coordinate-wise median of means whose number of buckets chosen according to the geometry of the loss, optimally tracks this phase transition in its expected risk minimax. We also show that natural projection-based median-of-means estimators for general norms, despite achieving the optimal confidence trade-off relative to the sample-mean benchmark of Lugosi and Mendelson (Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2019), can be polynomially suboptimal for $\ell_p$ norms even in the constant-probability regime.

papers.title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
papers.abstract: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circ\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.

papers.title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
papers.abstract: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

papers.title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
authors: Ryan Lim (Albert Einstein College of Medicine)
papers.abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

papers.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
papers.abstract: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-\alpha$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-\alpha$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-\beta})$, for some $\beta\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $\beta\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

papers.title: Rectifying Conformity Scores for Better Conditional Coverage
papers.abstract: We present a new method for generating confidence sets within the split conformal prediction framework. Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

papers.title: Distribution-free certificate of similarity between distributions with blurred total variation distance
papers.abstract: Classical two-sample tests aim to determine whether two distributions are equal or not based on samples from each one. Even in an distribution-free setting, well-known methods such as the permutation test can provide statistical evidence that the two distributions differ. However, failure to reject equality does not necessarily establish that they are similar. In this work, we study the complementary problem of certifying distributional similarity with finite-sample confidence, without imposing assumptions on the underlying distributions. We show, however, that for continuous distributions, any distribution-free upper confidence bound on the total variation (TV) distance must be trivial with high probability, even if the distributions are identical. Thus, certifying similarity in TV with a distribution-free guarantee is practically impossible. We therefore examine the blurred TV distance, a relaxation of TV distance that enables us to quantify similarity after applying a common blurring operation while retaining the interpretation of TV. We construct distribution-free upper and lower confidence bounds on blurred TV, establish their finite-sample validity, and examine its properties in high dimensions.

papers.title: Structural interpretability in SVMs with truncated orthogonal polynomial kernels
papers.abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs) can yield classifiers with similar predictive performance but different internal structures, particularly in the contributions of individual explanatory variables and their interactions. We introduce Orthogonal Representation Contribution Analysis (ORCA), a post-training methodology for SVMs constructed from tensor products of truncated Christoffel--Darboux kernels. The associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) admits a finite orthonormal polynomial basis in which the regularized component of the fitted decision function has an exact expansion. Squared expansion coefficients induce an additive decomposition of its squared RKHS norm. Based on this representation, normalized Orthogonal Kernel Contribution (OKC) indices quantify the fractions of the squared RKHS norm associated with total polynomial degrees, interaction orders, and input-variable contributions, both individually and through interactions of arbitrary order. ORCA summarizes these indices through joint structural maps, variable-specific displays, and comparisons of fitted classifiers. A controlled quartet of classification problems illustrates substantial structural differences under matched predictive performance. A double-spiral experiment compares five Jacobi kernels, while an application to the Vertebral Column data illustrates the method after cross-validated model selection. ORCA provides a quantitative characterization of the internal structure of fitted SVMs, revealing differences that may remain undetected by standard predictive performance metrics.

papers.title: Sharp High-Dimensional Gaussian Approximations over Rectangles without Covariance Restrictions
papers.abstract: We study how well a sum of $n$ independent random vectors with $p$ coordinates can be approximated by a Gaussian vector with the same mean and covariance. We measure the error over rectangles, so the bounds apply to maxima and simultaneous confidence regions. The coordinates may be arbitrarily dependent, even exactly linearly dependent, and the bounds do not deteriorate as the covariance matrix becomes singular. After standardizing the coordinate variances, bounded or sub-exponential coordinates give the $n^{-1/2}$ sample-size rate up to logarithmic factors, with the size or tail bounds held fixed. The main upper bounds retain the Gaussian expected maximum, improving the rates when the coordinates are strongly dependent. Fourth-moment refinements give further improvements when large observations contribute little to individual coordinate variances. If we instead impose a fixed moment bound of order $q>4$ on the largest absolute coordinate, together with a coordinate fourth-moment bound, the rate becomes $n^{-1/2+1/q}$ up to logarithmic factors. At $q=4$, the slower $n^{-1/4}$ rate is unavoidable, confirming our earlier conjecture. We also allow the bounds on observation size to grow with $n$. Lower-bound examples show that the dependence on sample size, observation size, and Gaussian width is sharp up to logarithmic factors in the regimes studied, and in several regimes the upper and lower bounds match including the logarithmic terms.

papers.title: Stochastic Multivariate Taylor Measure Functions
papers.abstract: We introduce stochastic multivariate Taylor measure functions (SMTMFs), which extend the multivariate Taylor measure function framework through random Taylor coefficients and a possibly random Taylor parameter. We establish their measurability properties and derive sufficient conditions for the associated processes to be martingales, including criteria based on conditional covariance and continuous semimartingale decompositions. We construct standard Brownian motion as an almost surely uniformly convergent limit of finite SMTMFs using the Levy-Ciesielski representation. We also show that the completion of the finite stochastic MTMF space under the expected uniform norm contains Brownian motion, Brownian bridges, fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H, and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes with integrable initial conditions. Our main result characterizes this completion as the Bochner space, under an admissibility condition on jointly measurable stochastic Taylor coefficients. The proof uses dyadic piecewise linear interpolation to approximate integrable continuous stochastic processes in the expected uniform norm. Thus, the completed SMTMF space encompasses the full class of integrable continuous random functions on a compact time interval.

papers.title: Incomplete U-Statistics of Equireplicate Designs: Berry-Esseen Bound and Efficient Construction
papers.abstract: U-statistics are a fundamental class of estimators that generalize the sample mean and underpin much of nonparametric statistics. Although extensively studied in both statistics and probability, key challenges remain: their high computational cost - addressed partly through incomplete U-statistics - and their non-standard asymptotic behavior in the degenerate case, which typically requires resampling methods for hypothesis testing. This paper presents a novel perspective on U-statistics, grounded in hypergraph theory and combinatorial designs. We identify the dependency graph of an incomplete U-statistic with the line graph of its design hypergraph and use Stein's method to derive Berry-Esseen bounds for deterministic designs under full degeneracy. We further extend these results to studentized statistics using a variance estimator tailored to the fully degenerate setting. The resulting bounds establish Gaussian limits for superlinear design sizes with fixed kernel order and accommodate diverging order under separate conditions. We also develop efficient algorithms for constructing equireplicate designs, a subclass of deterministic designs, which yield minimum-variance incomplete U-statistics in the second-order case. Beyond its theoretical contributions, our framework provides permutation-free alternatives to tests based on fully degenerate U-statistics, as demonstrated in experiments with the two-sample Maximum Mean Discrepancy test and a one-sample mean test based on a higher-order U-statistic.

papers.title: Structural functional identifiability and model discovery in differential equation models
papers.abstract: Differential equation models are widely used to describe, interpret, and predict dynamical phenomena across science and engineering. In practice, however, the governing dynamics are rarely fully known and must be inferred from observational data. Traditionally, inverse problems in differential equation modelling have focused on estimating unknown parameter values. In this setting, structural identifiability determines whether parameter values can, in principle, be uniquely recovered from ideal observations and is, therefore, a prerequisite for meaningful inference. More recently, the integration of machine learning with mechanistic modelling has enabled the discovery of unknown equations, functions, and constitutive relationships, substantially expanding the space of admissible models. This raises a fundamental question: under what conditions can unknown functional components be uniquely recovered from data? In this paper, we generalise the classical notion of structural parameter identifiability to functional identifiability. We first identify broad classes of models for which unique functional recovery is impossible. We then show how functional identifiability can be assessed for differential equation models using differential algebra-based techniques which are well-established as a means of assessing structural identifiability for ordinary differential equation models. Our framework reveals new phenomena that arise in the transition from parametric to function inference and have no analogue in the classical setting. Finally, we characterise functional identifiability in several common model classes. Taken together, our results demonstrate that functional identifiability provides a theoretical foundation for modern inverse problems in differential equation modelling, particularly those that use machine learning representations of unknown system components.

papers.title: Asymptotic efficiency of tests for quantum statistical models
papers.abstract: In classical statistics, local asymptotic normality provides a general framework for characterizing optimal testing power and constructing asymptotically efficient procedures. Extending this framework to quantum statistical models introduces additional challenges arising from the noncommutativity of observables and the need to optimize over quantum measurements. In this paper, we develop a theory of asymptotic efficiency for quantum hypothesis testing using quantum local asymptotic normality and the asymptotic representation theorem. We establish sharp nuisance-maximin power bounds for one-sided tests and two-sided tests within the unbiased class by reducing the corresponding classical--quantum Gaussian shift experiments to classical testing problems. This reduction is justified through a quantum Hunt--Stein argument that accommodates both commuting and noncommuting Gaussian coordinates. Under suitable asymptotic invariance conditions, the resulting bounds transfer to the original quantum experiments and are attained by scalar symmetric logarithmic derivative tests. We further develop a two-stage adaptive construction that achieves the same local asymptotic power without knowledge of the reference parameter. As an application, we study testing of smooth spectral functionals of quantum states. We compare scalar symmetric logarithmic derivative tests with the weak Schur sampling plug-in test and with optimally weighted linear statistics of its fluctuations. This comparison distinguishes loss from the plug-in weighting from a gap between the best such spectral statistic and the scalar score procedure. We characterize equality of the corresponding variances and illustrate the two gaps through explicit examples.

papers.title: Support recovery of diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis
papers.abstract: We study diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis with possibly large score estimation and discretization errors, and show that while they may not exactly recover the data distribution, they will exactly recover the support (or data manifold). In continuous time, we use a Lyapunov function to show that even if the relative score estimation error is fixed (and not necessarily vanishing), then the rate at which the process approaches the support is $O(\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|})$ as $t \to T$, where $T$ is the final time. In discrete time, we use geometric time steps with a fixed (non-vanishing) ratio and show that with a fixed (also not small) relative score estimation error, the process approaches the data manifold exponentially with the number of iterations. The proof relies on controlling a Gaussian measure of a neighborhood of the cut-locus of the data manifold, using a polynomial approximation argument combined with quantitative semi-algebraic estimates.

papers.title: Learning the Average Dose-Response Function with a Right-Censored Treatment
papers.abstract: This paper considers estimation and inference for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes for censored units. Using the duration lower bounds provided by censored records, we construct a novel multiply robust estimator through augmented local estimating equations. Under suitable regularity conditions, the estimator remains consistent when any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival function are consistently estimated. We establish its convergence rate and asymptotic distribution within a cross-fitting framework under appropriate conditions on nuisance estimation. To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.

papers.title: Structural latent dimension: deterministic geometry and local Fisher structure
papers.abstract: We study the \emph{structural dimension} of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight $b$-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.

papers.title: Nonparametric Classification under Adversarial Attacks: Decision-Boundary Geometry and Optimal Rates
papers.abstract: Unlike in continuous regression, a small input perturbation in classification can move an input across a decision boundary and flip the predicted label. Decision-boundary geometry is therefore essential to understanding adversarial classification risk. Under anisotropic smoothness and margin conditions, we quantify this geometric contribution and establish sharp minimax rates for adversarial excess risk relative to the ordinary Bayes risk. These rates comprise a statistical term governed by the harmonic mean smoothness and a geometric cost of adversarial perturbations governed by the least smooth direction. As smoothness and the margin exponent vary, the adversarial term exhibits a phase transition from a fractional power of the attack radius to linear scaling, with a logarithmic correction in a critical regime. In addition, we construct an adaptive classifier that attains these rates over a range of smoothness and margin classes. We further characterize the minimax rate for adversarial excess risk under a budget on ordinary excess risk, yielding an explicit trade-off curve. The curve identifies attack regimes where ordinary minimax optimality entails a suboptimal adversarial rate. Finally, numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.

papers.title: Markov potential priors for prediction in Gamma models
papers.abstract: We consider Bayesian prediction in independent Gamma scale models with arbitrary known positive shape parameters. When the dimension is at least three, we construct a shrinkage prior toward any prespecified positive scale vector. The resulting predictive density strictly dominates the Jeffreys predictive density under Kullback--Leibler loss and is minimax. The prior is obtained by weighting the Jeffreys prior with a Markov potential. The transition is determined by the beta--gamma decomposition. The domination result is nonasymptotic.

papers.title: Local asymptotic normality for Cox-Ingersoll-Ross drift parameters under high-frequency sampling and the strict Feller condition
papers.abstract: For the ergodic Cox--Ingersoll--Ross (CIR) diffusion with known diffusion scale and a fixed initial value, we prove local asymptotic normality (LAN) of the exactly sampled experiment for the drift parameters whenever the Feller index exceeds $1$, assuming only a vanishing mesh and a diverging observation horizon. This improves the previously known condition that the index exceed $(11+\sqrt{89})/2$. The proof cuts off the continuous score near $0$, recovers the remainder by exact conditional centering on each sampling interval, and transfers LAN by a conditional-likelihood argument.

papers.title: Asymptotic Divergence-Based Monitoring for Data Drift in Production AI Systems: A Discrete Case Approach
papers.abstract: We develop a complete asymptotic theory for monitoring data drift in production artificial intelligence (AI) systems whose inputs take values in a finite set of categories. The framework combines two complementary inferential tools. Under the no-drift hypothesis $H_0$, the two-sample likelihood-ratio statistic $G$ of Wilks follows a universal Chi_{r-1}^2 law, independently of the divergence chosen and of the sample sizes; the calibrated Population Stability Index (PSI) of Yurdakul and Naranjo (2021) shares the same Chi_{r-1}^2 limit and is asymptotically equivalent to the $G$-test under $H_0$. Under the drift hypothesis $H_1$, the plug-in phi-divergence is asymptotically normal with a variance computed in closed form for the one-sample, two-sample and symmetrized configurations, yielding standardized $Z$-statistics, detection boundaries, power functions and sample-size planning rules. We supply a per-category decomposition that localizes the drift on specific categories, a Benjamini--Hochberg procedure for monitoring many features simultaneously, and an explicit comparison with the heuristic PSI cut-offs of industrial practice. Two fully worked simulation examples - one one-sample with the R\'enyi divergence and multiple testing, one two-sample with the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and sample-size planning - illustrate every notion of the paper on realistic production data.

papers.title: On the false discovery rate of one-sided p-values under Gaussian dependence
papers.abstract: We study the false discovery rate (FDR) of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure for $K$ hypotheses at nominal level $q$ under Gaussian dependence of one-sided p-values. We ask whether the global null is least favorable after optimizing over correlation matrices. We show that the global null attains the worst-case FDR for $K\le3$ at every level. In dimension eight, an explicit mixed-null construction has FDR $21q/20$ for $0<q<1/2$. It exceeds the global-null maximum for all sufficiently small $q$, by a uniform extension of the known fixed-matrix small-level Simes bound. For $0<q<1/2$, we identify eight as the first inflation dimension in the monotone rank-one class and prove that $21q/20$ is its exact eight-dimensional maximum. In the same level range, the sharp multiplicative bound over all dimensions in this class is twice the omega constant $w = W(1)$, where $W$ is the Lambert $W$ function. This bound is approached as the dimension increases. We also give scale conditions for stability around the independence benchmark $m_0q/K$, where $m_0$ is the number of true nulls, and obtain a dimension-free upper bound of $q+q^2/2+O(q^3)$ at small levels under the global null with nonpositive correlations.

papers.title: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
papers.abstract: We study the computation of approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in arbitrary dimension $d\ge 1$ via the Fisher-Rao gradient flow. We provide a certified algorithm based on an entropic proximal discretization of the flow which, given a sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, returns an absolutely continuous mixing measure $\tilde\mu$ admitting an exact finite-dimensional representation and satisfying $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\tilde\mu})\le\varepsilon$. For almost every dataset $X_1,\cdots, X_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $n>2(d+1)(m+1)^2$, where $m$ is the number of support points of the NPMLE, the algorithm requires $O(n\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d+2}(1/\varepsilon))$ time. En route, we also establish results on the well-posedness and convergence properties of the continuous-time Fisher--Rao flow. In particular, initializing the flow at the uniform probability measure on a ball containing the convex hull of the observations, we show that $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\mu_t})=O(\log t/t)$. We also establish that, for almost every dataset satisfying the same condition on $n$ as above, the set of global maxima of the optimal score is the same as the support of the NPMLE, and the Hessian of the optimal score is nondegenerate at these points, extending a result of (Polyanskiy-Sellke, 2025) to higher dimensions.
